title: All, Most, Some and None: Groups and Of-Phrases
summary: Use quantifiers directly before general nouns, add of before a defined group or pronoun, and distinguish a general statement from a statement about specific people or things. Practise optional of after all/half with determiners, required of with object pronouns, and quantifiers used alone when the noun is understood.
learningObjectives: Distinguish quantifiers with general noun groups from quantifiers + of + a particular group.
Use all (of), most of, some of, any of, half (of) and none of accurately with determiners and demonstratives.
Include of before object pronouns such as us, them and it after quantifiers.
Use most, some, half and none without repeating an understood noun or group, preserving the intended reference.

explanation.heading: General groups: quantifier directly before a noun
explanation.body: Quantifiers such as all, most, some, any, many and few may modify a general plural or uncountable noun without of. All bicycles have brakes is a claim about bicycles generally; Most offices have meeting rooms is a general pattern. Do not insert of directly before an undetermined general noun: most of offices is not standard. No also goes directly before a noun: no tickets, no energy. The quantifier helps establish how broadly the sentence applies.
explanation.example: Most travellers prefer clear instructions before a journey.

explanation.heading: Specific groups: quantifier + of + determiner
explanation.body: When the group is identified by a determiner such as the, my, your, this or those, many quantifiers use of: some of the emails, most of my colleagues, none of these documents. This construction chooses a quantity from a known set. Compare Most requests arrive online, a general claim, with Most of the requests we received yesterday arrived online, a statement about a particular group. Do not omit of after most or none in this pattern.
explanation.example: Some of those tickets were reserved for students.

explanation.heading: All and half allow optional of before a determiner
explanation.body: Before the, my, this, these and similar determiners, both all and all of are possible: all the rooms / all of the rooms. Half also permits half the amount / half of the amount. This optionality does not extend to many other quantifiers: most my colleagues is incorrect; use most of my colleagues. In general statements without determiners, say all rooms, not all of rooms.
explanation.example: Half (of) the exhibition space is closed for renovation.

explanation.heading: Object pronouns require of
explanation.body: Before it, us, you and them, quantifiers such as all, some, half, most and none need of: all of us, some of it, half of them. Do not say all us or half it. A whole collection is all of them, while a selection is some of them. The pronoun must be appropriate for the group previously identified. Use none of it for uncountable content and none of them for a plural set.
explanation.example: We divided the presentation into four parts and reviewed two of them before lunch.

explanation.heading: Leave out an understood noun after a quantifier
explanation.body: A quantifier can stand alone when the noun is clear from earlier context: Some arrived late, but most were on time. None can stand alone as a short answer; most of them may be shortened to most where the group is unmistakable. Half can refer to a share of an understood quantity: half is for the organisers. Avoid the half in this use unless referring to a particular half already identified. Reference and context determine which group the quantifier describes.
explanation.example: We checked ten entries. Three needed corrections, but most were accurate.

comparisons.title: General statement versus a defined set

left.label: General group without of
left.note: Most modifies cafés in general; no of is needed.

right.label: Defined set with of
right.example: Most of the cafés on this street close early.
right.note: The phrase on this street identifies a particular group, so use of the.

comparisons.title: A determiner versus an object pronoun

left.label: All + determiner
left.example: All my teammates received the update.
left.note: All of my teammates would also be possible before my.

right.label: All + object pronoun
right.example: All of them received the update.
right.note: Of is mandatory before the object pronoun them.

comparisons.title: A known set versus an understood set

left.label: Group explicitly named
left.example: Some of these files need renaming.
left.note: Some of these selects files from a particular known set.

right.label: Noun omitted after mention
right.example: I examined the files, and some need renaming.
right.note: Some stands alone because files has already been mentioned.

examples.sentence: All electric kettles need a power source.
examples.note: All directly introduces the general plural noun kettles.

examples.sentence: Most of the interns in this group have finished their orientation.
examples.note: Of the interns refers to a specific, identified group.

examples.sentence: None of this material is suitable for outdoor use.
examples.note: None of selects zero of an uncountable amount identified by this.

examples.sentence: Half my workday is usually spent in meetings.
examples.note: Half can omit of when followed by my.

examples.sentence: The students watched the demonstration, but not all of them understood it.
examples.note: Of is required before them even after all.

examples.sentence: I sorted six reports: some were complete, and the rest needed changes.
examples.note: Some stands alone because reports is already understood.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Most of commuters take the bus here.
commonMistakes.correct: Most commuters take the bus here.
commonMistakes.why: Do not insert of directly before a general plural noun with no determiner.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Some these invitations contain the wrong date.
commonMistakes.correct: Some of these invitations contain the wrong date.
commonMistakes.why: Use some of before the demonstrative these.

commonMistakes.incorrect: All us signed the attendance sheet.
commonMistakes.correct: All of us signed the attendance sheet.
commonMistakes.why: An object pronoun such as us must follow of after all.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Most my colleagues will join the call.
commonMistakes.correct: Most of my colleagues will join the call.
commonMistakes.why: Unlike all or half, most needs of before the possessive determiner my.

studyTips: Underline the noun phrase after each quantifier; ask whether it refers to a general category, a defined group, or an object pronoun.
Practise three pairs: most restaurants / most of these restaurants, all my notes / all of my notes, half the budget / half of the budget.
In a two-sentence summary, name a group once and replace it with some, most, none or all of them as appropriate.

exercises.prompt: The survey describes people in general: ___ adults use messaging apps every day.
exercises.feedback: Most directly modifies the general plural noun adults; most of needs an identified group.

exercises.prompt: The conference sent invitations to a named group of twenty speakers. ___ those speakers accepted.
exercises.feedback: Those identifies a particular group, so most of those speakers is required.

exercises.prompt: We interviewed eight candidates, and ___ had the required certificate. The other candidates were still in training.
exercises.feedback: Half of them correctly refers to four of the eight known candidates; of is required before them.

exercises.prompt: The museum checked its five security cameras. ___ them were working; every camera needed repair.
exercises.feedback: None of them identifies zero cameras within the known group of five.

exercises.prompt: ___ patients need clear information about their treatment. (one word: general statement about every patient)
exercises.feedback: All directly modifies the general plural noun patients.

exercises.prompt: ___ the emails in yesterday’s batch were sent twice. (two words: more than half of a specific group)
exercises.feedback: Most of the emails refers to a defined collection from yesterday.

exercises.prompt: The friends paid for dinner together, and all ___ them contributed equally. (one word required before a pronoun)
exercises.feedback: The structure all of them requires of before the object pronoun them.

exercises.prompt: ___ my annual leave is already booked. (one word: 50%; omit optional of)
exercises.feedback: Half my annual leave is grammatical; half of my annual leave is also possible but the prompt requires the form without of.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence by removing the unnecessary word: Most of museums display objects in carefully controlled conditions.
acceptedAnswers: Most museums display objects in carefully controlled conditions.
exercises.feedback: The sentence makes a general claim about museums; omit of before an undetermined noun.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: None the tickets for tonight’s performance remain available.
acceptedAnswers: None of the tickets for tonight’s performance remain available.
exercises.feedback: None needs of before the defined noun group the tickets.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: All them completed the safety briefing.
acceptedAnswers: All of them completed the safety briefing.
exercises.feedback: Use all of them, with of required before an object pronoun.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: Most our training materials are available online.
acceptedAnswers: Most of our training materials are available online.
exercises.feedback: Most needs of before the possessive determiner our.

speakingExercises.prompt: Make one general statement using these exact words: most / libraries / offer / digital catalogues. Start with “Most”.
speakingExercises.feedback: Most directly modifies a general plural noun without of.

speakingExercises.prompt: Use “some of” to make one statement about this defined set: the eight reports / need revisions. Begin with “Some of”.
acceptedAnswers: Some of the eight reports need revisions.
speakingExercises.feedback: The eight reports identifies a known set, so use some of.

speakingExercises.prompt: Restate “The complete team attended” using the exact subject “All of them”. Use the past tense attended.
speakingExercises.feedback: Of is required before them after all.

speakingExercises.prompt: You are describing 50 percent of a known amount. Say: “Half of the budget” + “is reserved for transport”.
acceptedAnswers: Half of the budget is reserved for transport.
speakingExercises.feedback: Half of the budget is grammatical; the expression refers to a specified budget.

speakingExercises.prompt: Compare a general rule with one event. Say one sentence from the words: most / trains / have / several carriages. Do not use “of”.
speakingExercises.feedback: A general category follows most directly, without of.

speakingExercises.prompt: Five documents were checked, and zero were missing. Begin with “None of” and end with “were missing”. Use the pronoun “them”.
speakingExercises.feedback: None of them selects zero documents from a known plural set; plural agreement is natural.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two sentences. Facts: the museum owns ten paintings; some / be / on display. Use the present simple in both and do not repeat “paintings” in sentence two.
acceptedAnswers: The museum owns ten paintings. Some are on display.
speakingExercises.feedback: Some stands alone in the second sentence because paintings is already understood.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct the quantifier expression, changing nothing else: “Most my classmates enjoy group projects.”
acceptedAnswers: Most of my classmates enjoy group projects.
speakingExercises.feedback: Most needs of before the possessive determiner my.

listeningExercises.audioText: Most commuters in this city travel by bus, but most of the passengers on this particular bus are tourists.
choices: A general commuting pattern and the passengers on one specific bus.
The cost of tickets on two buses.
Tourists and commuters who never use buses.
listeningExercises.feedback: Most commuters refers to a general population; most of the passengers selects a specific group.

listeningExercises.audioText: All of our presentation slides are ready, although half of them still need a final spelling check.
choices: Creating every slide from the beginning.
Checking the spelling on half the slides.
Replacing all slides with new photographs.
listeningExercises.feedback: Half of them refers to half of the slides already mentioned.

listeningExercises.audioText: Some of the visitors joined the morning workshop, while the rest explored the garden.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word quantifier immediately before “the visitors”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Some of selects an unspecified portion of a defined group.

listeningExercises.audioText: We reviewed six proposals. None was rejected outright, but two will need more information.
listeningExercises.prompt: How many proposals were rejected immediately?
listeningExercises.feedback: None was rejected outright indicates zero immediate rejections.

listeningExercises.audioText: Most office equipment is supplied by the company, but employees purchase some of their own accessories.
listeningExercises.prompt: What are employees responsible for purchasing?
listeningExercises.feedback: Some of their own accessories names a subset purchased by employees.

listeningExercises.audioText: I have read half of the handbook, and I will finish the other half tomorrow.
listeningExercises.prompt: How far has the speaker progressed?
choices: One of two equal parts has been read.
Only the introduction has been read.
listeningExercises.feedback: Half of the handbook expresses one of two equal shares.

listeningExercises.audioText: Every seat was taken, and all of us had to stand near the entrance.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word expression heard immediately before “had to stand”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Of is required before us after all.

listeningExercises.audioText: The organisers contacted ten speakers, but most of them were already busy.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word phrase heard immediately before “were already busy”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Most of them refers to a majority within the known group of ten speakers.
